summary: Specifies the addition of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), chosen by NIST, to the Kerberos cryptosystem suite. AES is described as faster and, it is believed, more secure than the older DES algorithm.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3962 adds AES encryption and checksum types to Kerberos 5. It defines how pass phrases become keys and how ciphertext stealing handles messages without adding padding in most cases.

questions: how does kerberos derive an aes key from a password
what is the default pbkdf2 iteration count in kerberos
subtitle: AES encryption and checksums for Kerberos 5, with keys derived from pass phrases.

tldr.problem: Kerberos 5 needs encryption and checksum types based on the Advanced Encryption Standard.
tldr.mechanism: The specification defines AES with 128-bit or 256-bit keys, PBKDF2 plus a derivation step for pass phrases, and CBC ciphertext stealing to avoid message expansion.
tldr.outcome: It assigns encryption types 17 and 18 and checksum types 15 and 16. RFC 3962 is updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3962 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2005 and is updated by RFC 9141.

sections.title: AES Types for Kerberos
sections.content:
RFC 3962 defines Kerberos 5 encryption key and checksum types using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). The types support 128-bit blocks and keys of 128 or 256 bits.

The specification uses AES with ciphertext stealing to avoid message expansion and uses SHA-1 for the associated checksum function. It follows the simplified cryptographic profile in RFC 3961.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos 5 can use AES with either a 128-bit or 256-bit key. This RFC also defines the matching checksum types and their operation.

sections.title: Creating Keys from Pass Phrases
sections.content:
A random key is generated by copying the required amount of random data. To make a key from a pass phrase and salt, PBKDF2 with a SHA-1 HMAC produces an intermediate key, which is passed to the DK function with the eight-octet string kerberos.

The iteration count is a four-octet unsigned big-endian number. If no parameter is supplied, the default is 00 00 10 00, or 4,096 iterations. A zero parameter value represents 2**32 iterations.
sections.plainLanguage: For a pass phrase, PBKDF2 repeatedly combines the phrase and salt to make an intermediate key. A further derivation step produces the Kerberos key, and the iteration count tells both sides how much work to perform.

sections.title: CBC Ciphertext Stealing
sections.content:
Kerberos uses cipher block chaining (CBC) with ciphertext stealing for a possibly partial final block. This avoids the message expansion that ordinary CBC padding can cause for messages of arbitrary size.

For exactly one full block, AES encrypts that block directly. Input shorter than one block is padded to one block, but padding values are unspecified and protocols must not rely on them. Ciphertext stealing is used for the last two blocks, including when the message length is a multiple of the block size.
sections.plainLanguage: Ciphertext stealing handles a partial final block without adding a full padding block in most cases. A message shorter than one block is padded, but the padding value is not fixed.

sections.title: Algorithm Parameters and Numbers
sections.content:
The profile uses AES in CBC-CTS mode with a 16-octet block, SHA-1, and a 12-octet HMAC output. It defines encryption type 17 for aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 and type 18 for aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96.

The corresponding checksum types are 15 and 16, each with a 96-bit output. These checksum types are used with their corresponding encryption types.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile assigns separate identifiers to the two key sizes and their matching checksums. Implementations use the identifiers to select the same algorithm parameters.

sections.title: Pass Phrase and Length Risks
sections.content:
A pass phrase does not necessarily provide the entropy suggested by a 256-bit derived key. Increasing PBKDF2 iterations increases the work for an attacker, but also increases the work for a legitimate client; a spoofed response with a very large count can consume client CPU.

Implementations may cap iteration counts, and the cap should be no less than 50,000. A new random salt when passwords change limits reuse of cached work. Ciphertext stealing also reveals the exact message length in most cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A long derived key cannot make a weak pass phrase unpredictable. More iterations slow guessing but also slow legitimate users, and ciphertext length remains visible.
